name: Cephalandra Indica
scientificName: Coccinia grandis (synonyms: Coccinia indica, Cephalandra indica)
origin: Native to India and tropical Asia; also found in tropical Africa
habitat: A climbing vine of tropical and subtropical regions, often growing wild on fences and trees
partUsed: Fresh leaves and aerial parts; the fruit and root are also used in traditional practice
preparation: Mother tincture prepared from the fresh plant; also used in low attenuations in traditional Indian practice
alkaloids: Traces of an alkaloid reported in the plant
generalAnalysis: A remedy that comes from Indian clinical practice rather than the classical provings of Boericke or Clarke. Its traditional picture is built around profuse urination with exhaustion, intense thirst, dryness of the mouth and burning sensations relieved by cold, together with recurrent boils and carbuncles. It is studied chiefly for its traditional association with the diabetic symptom picture, which must not be confused with evidence of treatment.

drugPicture.generalPicture: A picture of fluid loss and burning: the patient passes large quantities of urine and feels exhausted afterwards, is very thirsty for large draughts of water, has a dry burning mouth and a burning sensation over the body that cold applications relieve. Boils and carbuncles may recur, and giddiness is worse after urination.
